title: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
summary: How a Microsoft cloud tenant is attacked and defended: apps and consent, device code phishing, PRTs and token theft, Conditional Access gaps, hybrid Tier 0, logs and response.
outcomes: Explain how a tenant, its tokens, app registrations and service principals fit together, and where Global Administrator power hides
Distinguish delegated from application permissions and judge the risk of a consent grant
Trace Midnight Blizzard, Storm-2372 and Octo Tempest intrusions step by step and name the control that breaks each
Explain refresh tokens, PRTs, CAE and Token Protection, and how long a stolen token keeps working
Find the gaps in a Conditional Access policy set: service principals, exclusions, device code and legacy auth
Treat Entra Connect, PTA agents, the Seamless SSO key and AD FS as Tier 0 and harden them
Investigate with sign-in, audit, Graph activity and MailItemsAccessed logs, and run a containment runbook

lessons.title: A tenant: the cloud directory behind every Microsoft 365 login

blocks.md:
Ravi works at a company of 3,000 people. At 08:55 Ravi opens Outlook, Teams and a OneDrive folder, and never types a password after the first one. Behind those apps sits one thing: the company's **Microsoft Entra ID tenant**, the cloud directory that knows Ravi, Ravi's groups, Ravi's laptop and every app allowed to act for Ravi.

The Active Directory attacks course ended at the edge of the on-premises domain. This course crosses that edge. Most companies that run Windows also run Microsoft 365, and Microsoft's documentation says every Microsoft 365, Azure or Dynamics CRM Online subscriber is already using Entra ID: every tenant is automatically an Entra tenant. Win the tenant and you win mail, files, chat and often the Azure subscriptions too.

The words, used through the whole course:

- **Microsoft Entra ID**: Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service, called Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) until Microsoft renamed it in 2023. It authenticates users, devices and apps, enforces policy and issues tokens.
- **Tenant**: one organisation's own instance of Entra ID, with its own users, groups, apps and policies. It has an immutable GUID (globally unique identifier), the **tenant ID**, and an initial domain such as `contoso.onmicrosoft.com`; the company adds its own domains later.
- **Microsoft 365** (M365): Microsoft's suite of cloud services. The parts that hold data are **Exchange Online** (hosted mail), **SharePoint Online** and **OneDrive** (files) and **Teams** (chat and meetings).
- **Microsoft Graph**: one web API at `graph.microsoft.com` through which apps read and change directory objects, mail, files and chats.

**How this differs from Active Directory.** An on-premises domain speaks Kerberos, NTLM and LDAP inside a network, and a domain controller holds the keys. A tenant speaks HTTPS and the protocols of the API, OAuth and JWT course and the federation course: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and SAML. There is no network to be inside of. Any device on the internet can reach `login.microsoftonline.com`, the sign-in endpoint, and every service behind it trusts one thing: a token signed by Entra ID.

So the security questions change shape. Not "who can reach the DC?" but "who can get a token, for which app, with which permissions, and how long does it last?" (For legacy software that still needs Kerberos or LDAP in the cloud, Microsoft sells a separate managed domain, Entra Domain Services; it is not the tenant itself.)

blocks.title: One tenant, one token issuer, many services that trust it

scenes.caption: Ravi signs in once to the tenant. The tenant is the only party that checks a password or an MFA prompt.
Each Microsoft 365 service accepts a token signed by Entra ID for that service. None of them checks Ravi's password.
Apps are identities too. A third-party app gets its own tokens and calls Microsoft Graph, which reaches the same mail and files.
In most companies the users come from on-premises AD through a sync server. That link makes the on-premises domain part of the cloud's attack surface (lesson 11).
Everything converges on the tenant: whoever controls it, or can mint its tokens, controls every service on the right.

blocks.md:
**What is inside a token.** Recall the JWT anatomy from the API, OAuth and JWT course. Entra ID's access tokens carry claims you will see in every investigation (from Microsoft's access token claims reference):

- `aud`: the resource the token is for (for example Microsoft Graph).
- `tid`: the tenant the user signed in to. `oid`: the immutable object ID of the user or service principal.
- `azp` (v2.0 tokens) or `appid` (v1.0): the client app using the token.
- `scp`: delegated permissions (scopes), present only in user tokens. `roles`: application permissions in app-only tokens, or the app roles assigned to a user.
- `amr`: how the subject authenticated, such as password plus MFA.
- `wids`: the tenant-wide admin roles of the user, when the app asks for them.

blocks.code:
import base64, json

def b64url_json(segment):
    pad = "=" * (-len(segment) % 4)
    return json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(segment + pad))

def make(claims):  # toy: build an unsigned payload segment for the demo
    raw = json.dumps(claims).encode()
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(raw).rstrip(b"=").decode()

user_token = make({"aud": "https://graph.microsoft.com",
                   "tid": "6f1c0d2e-tenant-guid", "oid": "a91b-user-ana",
                   "azp": "1b73-mail-client", "scp": "Mail.Read User.Read",
                   "amr": ["pwd", "mfa"]})
app_token = make({"aud": "https://graph.microsoft.com",
                  "tid": "6f1c0d2e-tenant-guid", "oid": "c04e-sp-backup",
                  "azp": "77d2-backup-app", "roles": ["Mail.Read"]})

for name, seg in [("user token", user_token), ("app-only token", app_token)]:
    c = b64url_json(seg)
    who = "user + app" if "scp" in c else "app alone"
    perms = c.get("scp") or " ".join(c.get("roles", []))
    print(f"{name:15} tenant={c['tid'][:8]} subject={c['oid']:15} acts as {who:10} perms={perms}")

# Output:
# user token      tenant=6f1c0d2e subject=a91b-user-ana   acts as user + app perms=Mail.Read User.Read
# app-only token  tenant=6f1c0d2e subject=c04e-sp-backup  acts as app alone  perms=Mail.Read
blocks.caption: Decoding two toy token payloads (unsigned, for illustration; IDs shortened). The same permission name means different things: in `scp` the app acts for one user, in `roles` it acts alone (lesson 4).

blocks.md: Misconception: Entra ID is just Active Directory hosted by Microsoft. It has no domain controllers you can reach, no Group Policy and no Kerberos for cloud apps. Its trust runs on signed tokens over HTTPS, so its attacks are token, consent and policy attacks, not the ticket attacks of the AD course.
A tenant is a token issuer that many services trust. The questions that decide its security are: who can get a token, for which app, with which permissions, from where, and for how long.

blocks.question: An attacker has Ravi's Exchange Online access token. Which claim tells a defender which application obtained it?
options: `azp` (or `appid` in v1.0 tokens), the client application ID
`tid`, because it names the tenant
`aud`, because it names the application
`amr`, because it records the app's sign-in method
blocks.explain: `azp` (v2.0) or `appid` (v1.0) identify the client using the token. `aud` names the resource the token is for (Exchange Online here), `tid` the tenant and `amr` how the user authenticated. Investigations use `azp` or `appid` to spot an unexpected client.

blocks.question: Why do Microsoft 365 services not need to see a user's password?
options: They store a copy of each password hash
They use Kerberos tickets from the on-premises domain
They trust tokens signed by the tenant's Entra ID, which did the authentication
They ask the user's device for a certificate on every request
blocks.explain: Exchange, SharePoint and Teams are relying parties: they validate a token Entra ID signed for them. That is why a stolen or forged token is as good as a login, the theme of lessons 6 to 9.

lessons.title: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM

blocks.md:
In AD the prize was Domain Admins. In a tenant it is **Global Administrator**, which Microsoft's built-in roles reference describes as able to manage all aspects of Entra ID and of Microsoft services that use Entra identities. The cloud IAM course showed two more facts: the person who creates a tenant becomes its first Global Administrator, and a Global Administrator can give themselves control of every Azure subscription in the tenant.

Recall the split from that course. **Entra roles** govern the directory (users, apps, policies). **Azure roles** govern Azure resources such as VMs. This lesson is about Entra roles, because they decide who can change identities, and identities reach everything else.

Global Administrator is not the only door. Microsoft marks a set of roles as **privileged** because each can lead to elevation of privilege. The ones attackers aim for:

- **Privileged Role Administrator**: manages role assignments and all of PIM (below), so it can make anyone a Global Administrator.
- **Privileged Authentication Administrator**: can view, set and reset authentication methods, including passwords, for any user, administrators included.
- **Application Administrator** and **Cloud Application Administrator**: manage app registrations and enterprise apps. Microsoft warns that holders can add credentials to an application and then act as that application's identity, which is an elevation of privilege if the app holds powerful permissions.
- **Hybrid Identity Administrator**: configures sync and federation with on-premises AD (lesson 11).
- **Helpdesk Administrator**: resets passwords and invalidates refresh tokens, but only for non-administrators and some roles. That limit is deliberate (lesson 12).

blocks.title: Which role can reach Global Administrator power? (1 = directly)

scenes.caption: Global Administrator holds every column. It is the tenant's Domain Admins.
Privileged Role Administrator can assign roles, so it can create a new Global Administrator.
Privileged Authentication Administrator can reset a Global Administrator's password and MFA, then sign in as them.
Application Administrator can add a secret to an app that holds high application permissions and use them. The app is the escalation path.
Hybrid Identity Administrator changes sync and federation, the bridge to on-premises AD. Helpdesk Administrator, limited to non-admins, has no direct path.

blocks.md:
**Fewer, shorter, harder to use.** Microsoft's guidance on privileged roles gives concrete numbers: keep **fewer than 5** Global Administrators and **fewer than 10** privileged role assignments, require MFA for every admin, review assignments regularly and use just-in-time access.

**PIM** (Privileged Identity Management, Entra's service for managing and monitoring privileged access) provides that just-in-time access. A role can be assigned as **eligible** instead of **active**. An eligible admin holds no power until they **activate** the role, for a limited time, with MFA, a justification and optionally an approver. Microsoft notes there is no difference in the access an eligible or permanent assignment gives once active; the difference is that the power is absent most of the time, so a stolen admin session at 03:00 usually finds nothing to use.

**Emergency access accounts.** If MFA, federation or PIM approvals break, administrators can lock themselves out. Microsoft's guidance is to keep **two or more** emergency ("break glass") accounts: cloud-only accounts on the `*.onmicrosoft.com` domain, never federated or synced from on-premises, protected by a phishing-resistant method such as a FIDO2 passkey or certificate-based authentication, with the Global Administrator role permanently active. They are excluded from Conditional Access policies that could block them, because their strong credential is their protection, and their use should be rare and alerted on.

**The control plane.** Microsoft's enterprise access model renames Tier 0 as the **control plane**, and its guidance says any system that can manage or broker access to privileged roles is part of it: privileged access tools, jump hosts, automation runbooks and service principals that hold high privileges.

blocks.code:
# Read-only review with Microsoft Graph PowerShell (run from an admin workstation).
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "RoleManagement.Read.Directory"

# Global Administrator's role template ID (from Microsoft's built-in roles reference)
$ga = "62e90394-69f5-4237-9190-012177145e10"

# Who holds it permanently (active) ...
Get-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleAssignment -Filter "roleDefinitionId eq '$ga'" |
  Select-Object PrincipalId

# ... and who can activate it through PIM (eligible)
Get-MgRoleManagementDirectoryRoleEligibilitySchedule -Filter "roleDefinitionId eq '$ga'" |
  Select-Object PrincipalId

# Expect: 2+ emergency accounts active, a handful of humans eligible, and
# no service principal or synced (on-premises) account in either list.
blocks.caption: A role review (not run here; it needs a tenant). The last comment is the target state from Microsoft's guidance.

blocks.md: A service principal can hold an Entra admin role, and Microsoft names those that do as control plane assets. An app with Global Administrator, or with permission to assign roles, is a Global Administrator that has no MFA prompt to bypass. Review apps in role assignments with the same care as people.

Count who can become Global Administrator, not only who is one: role assigners, admin credential resetters, app credential managers and hybrid identity admins. Keep the count small, make it eligible rather than active, and keep two tested emergency accounts outside it.

blocks.question: A tenant has 3 Global Administrators, all eligible through PIM, but 14 users hold Application Administrator permanently, and one app they manage has the Graph permission RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory. What is the real number of paths to Global Administrator power?
options: 3: only the Global Administrators
0: PIM eligibility blocks all paths
14: but only if those users also hold Helpdesk Administrator
At least 17: any Application Administrator can add a credential to that app and use its permission to assign roles
blocks.explain: Microsoft's role reference warns that Application Administrators can add credentials to an app and act as it. An app with RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory can assign roles, so each of the 14 is a path, plus the 3 eligible admins.

blocks.question: Why should emergency access accounts be cloud-only and not synced from on-premises AD?
options: Synced accounts cannot hold the Global Administrator role
So that an outage or compromise of on-premises AD or federation cannot block or take over the last way into the tenant
Because cloud-only accounts do not need MFA
Because PIM only works for cloud-only accounts
blocks.explain: Microsoft's guidance keeps emergency access for cloud and for on-premises separate, with no dependency between them. If they were synced or federated, the failure they exist for (federation down, AD compromised) would take them down too.

lessons.title: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity

blocks.md:
A company buys an HR app from a vendor called Adatum and lets it read staff profiles. Where does "the HR app" live in the company's tenant? Entra ID answers with two objects, and confusing them is behind many cloud intrusions.

- The **application object** (what the portal calls an **app registration**) lives in exactly one tenant, the app's **home tenant**, here Adatum's. Microsoft compares it to a class in object-oriented programming: a template with the app's name, its **client ID** (also called app ID, globally unique), its redirect URIs, the permissions it asks for, and its **credentials** (client secrets and certificates).
- A **service principal** (the portal's **enterprise application**) is the app's local instance in each tenant that uses it. Microsoft says it defines what the app can actually do in that tenant, who can access it, and which resources it may reach. A multitenant app gets a service principal in every tenant where someone consents to it.

Two more kinds of service principal matter:

- **Managed identity** service principals, the Azure workload identities from the cloud IAM course. They have no application object and no credential anyone can read.
- **Legacy** service principals, created before app registrations existed; they can hold credentials and work only in their own tenant.

Microsoft's own services, such as Exchange Online and Microsoft Graph, also appear in every customer tenant as service principals. Microsoft calls its own apps **first-party** apps; everything else is third-party.

blocks.title: One application object, a service principal in each tenant using it

nodes.label:
HR app object
client ID, credentials

scenes.caption: Adatum registers the HR app once. The application object, its client ID and its credentials live only in Adatum's tenant.
Contoso's admin consents, so Contoso gets its own service principal, with the permissions Contoso granted.
Fabrikam's users consent for themselves, so Fabrikam's service principal holds different, user-level grants. Same app, different power per tenant.
The app proves who it is with a credential on the application object. Whoever can add a credential there can act as the app in every tenant that trusts it.
Defender's split: the home tenant guards the app's credentials and owners; each customer tenant guards what its service principal was granted.

blocks.caption: A toy model of the split (simplified: real service principals can also hold their own credentials). Authentication comes from the application object; authorization comes from the service principal in the target tenant.

blocks.md:
**Why attackers love apps.** An app's credential is a secret or certificate, not a human password: no MFA prompt, no user risk score, often a long expiry. Apps that hold **application permissions** (lesson 4) can read every mailbox or change the directory without any user present. And Conditional Access policies scoped to users do not apply to service principals (lesson 10).

The attack patterns that follow are all forms of one move: **get a credential onto an app that already holds power**, or **give power to an app you already control**. MITRE ATT&CK (the MITRE Corporation's public catalogue of attacker techniques) lists adding credentials to a cloud app as T1098.001, Additional Cloud Credentials.

**Defender view.** Each step leaves an Entra audit log entry (lesson 13). The activities to alert on, with names from Microsoft's audit activity reference: *Add service principal credentials*, *Update application - Certificates and secrets management*, *Add owner to application*, *Add application* and *Add service principal* by unusual actors, and *Add app role assignment to service principal* for high-risk permissions.

**Prevention.** Keep owners and Application Administrators few. Prefer certificates or federated credentials (workload identity federation, from the keyless pipelines lesson of the cloud course) over client secrets. Remove unused apps and expired credentials. And in an incident Microsoft advises **disabling** a malicious app rather than deleting it: a deleted service principal can return the next time someone consents, a disabled one cannot get tokens.

Misconception: deleting a malicious app from Enterprise applications removes it for good. Deleting the service principal removes this tenant's instance; the application object lives in the attacker's tenant, and any user who consents again recreates the service principal. Disable it so it cannot obtain tokens or be consented to.

An app is defined once (application object, home tenant) and instantiated per tenant (service principal). Credentials live with the definition, permissions with the instance. Anyone who can add a credential to a powerful app becomes that app.

blocks.question: A SaaS vendor's own tenant is breached, and the attacker adds a new client secret to the vendor's multitenant application object. Your tenant granted that app's service principal Mail.Read (application). What is your exposure?
options: None: the secret was added in another tenant
Only mailboxes of users who signed in to the app
The attacker can get app-only tokens for your tenant and read every mailbox the permission covers, until you disable the service principal or remove the grant
None, because application permissions need MFA
blocks.explain: The app authenticates with credentials on its application object, wherever that lives, and is authorized by your service principal's grants. Your controls are on your side: the grant, and disabling the service principal.

blocks.question: Which audit activity best catches someone quietly taking over an existing powerful app in your tenant?
options: Update application - Certificates and secrets management (or Add service principal credentials)
Add user
Consent to application
Register device
blocks.explain: Taking over an existing app means adding a credential to it, which logs as a certificates and secrets update on the application or added service principal credentials. Consent and new users are other steps of other patterns.

lessons.title: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent

blocks.md:
The API, OAuth and JWT course taught scopes and consent phishing. Entra ID adds a distinction that decides how bad a grant is. Microsoft's permissions overview defines two kinds of access:

- **Delegated access**: the app acts *on behalf of a signed-in user*, with **delegated permissions** (scopes). Both the app and the user must be authorized, so the app can never reach anything the user could not. An app granted `Files.Read.All` delegated reads only the files that user can read.
- **App-only access**: the app acts *as itself*, with no user, using **application permissions** (Microsoft also calls them app roles). An app granted `Files.Read.All` as an application permission can read every file in the tenant through Microsoft Graph.

blocks.title: Same permission name, two very different reaches

scenes.caption: Four mailboxes exist. Ana can read only Ana's own; Raj, the CEO's delegate, can also read the CEO's.
Delegated Mail.Read for Ana: the result is the intersection of what the app was granted and what Ana may read.
Delegated for Raj: the app inherits Raj's access, including the CEO's mailbox. A consent phish against a delegate reaches further than one against an intern.
Application Mail.Read: no user, no intersection. Every mailbox the permission covers.

blocks.md:
**Who may consent.** Consent is the act of granting those permissions, and Entra records it as a grant on the service principal.

- **User consent**: a user grants delegated permissions for themselves. Microsoft's documentation says that **by default** all users can consent to permissions that do not require an administrator, for example letting an app read their own mailbox.
- **Admin consent**: an administrator grants for the whole organisation. Application permissions, and many high-privilege delegated ones, can only be granted by an administrator. In consent exports, a delegated grant for everyone shows the consent type **AllPrincipals**.

Microsoft's incident response playbook for illicit consent lists the delegated permissions seen in consent phishing: `Mail.*`, `Contacts.*`, `MailboxSettings.*`, `People.*`, `Files.*`, `Notes.*`, `Directory.AccessAsUser.All` and Azure's `user_impersonation`. It reports that attackers used a combination of the first six in 99% of consent phishing attacks. Its highest-impact list adds `Application.ReadWrite.All`, `Directory.ReadWrite.All`, `RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory` and every application permission with write access.

blocks.prompt: Your tenant still uses the default user consent setting. A user clicks a link and is asked to let 'Invoice Viewer' read their mail and keep access (offline_access). Will Entra require an admin before the app gets tokens?
blocks.reveal:
Usually **no**. `Mail.Read` delegated does not require admin consent, so under the default setting the user can grant it, and `offline_access` gives the app a refresh token that keeps working without the user present.

Two exceptions can intervene: Microsoft's **risk-based step-up consent**, on by default when user consent is allowed, turns a request Microsoft detects as risky into one that needs admin approval; and your own consent policy can be stricter. That is why the recommended setting is to restrict user consent rather than rely on detection.

blocks.md:
**Settings that shrink the risk**, from Microsoft's consent guidance:

1. Allow user consent only for apps from **verified publishers** (publishers Microsoft has verified through a partner programme) or registered in your own tenant, and only for permissions you classify as **low impact** (such as `User.Read`, `openid`, `profile`, `email`). Microsoft's built-in policy for this is `microsoft-user-default-low`.
2. Turn on the **admin consent workflow**, so a blocked user can request an app and an admin reviews it instead of the user shopping for workarounds.
3. Review existing grants regularly; Microsoft's playbook says to look hardest at non-Microsoft apps with AllPrincipals grants and read-write or `.All` permissions.

**Detection.** The Entra audit activity *Consent to application* (with *IsAdminConsent* in its details), *Add delegated permission grant*, and *Add app role assignment to service principal* for application permissions. The playbook notes audit entries can take 30 minutes to 24 hours to appear in search, and that without auditing enabled beforehand there is nothing to investigate.

Misconception: an attacker needs an admin to consent before an app can steal mail. Delegated mail and file permissions are user-consentable by default, and the user's own mailbox is often the prize. Admin consent is needed for the tenant-wide versions, which is why attackers who compromise an admin go straight for application permissions.

Delegated means the app is capped by the user; application means the app is capped only by the permission. Restrict who may consent to what, and treat every application permission, especially any with write access, as an admin role held by software.

blocks.question: An app holds `Mail.Read` as a delegated permission, consented by Raj, who is a delegate on the CEO's mailbox. What can the app read with Raj's token?
options: Only Raj's mailbox, because delegated permissions are per-user
Every mailbox, because `Mail.Read` covers all mail
Nothing until an admin consents
Raj's mailbox and the CEO's, because delegated access is the intersection of the app's grant and Raj's own rights
blocks.explain: Delegated access can never exceed the user's rights, but it equals them where the grant covers it. Raj can read the CEO's mail, so an app acting for Raj can too. This is why consent phishing targets assistants and delegates.

blocks.question: Which grant should an investigator treat as the most dangerous in a review of consent grants?
options: User.Read delegated, consented by one user
Mail.ReadWrite as an application permission on a non-Microsoft app nobody recognises
openid and profile for a verified Microsoft app
Files.Read delegated, consented by one user
blocks.explain: Application permissions work without any user and cover the whole tenant, and write access lets the app change or send mail. Microsoft's playbook places app-only versions of the Mail permissions, and all write-capable app-only permissions, at the top of the review list.

lessons.title: Case: Midnight Blizzard inside Microsoft's own tenant (2024)

blocks.md:
On 12 January 2024 Microsoft's security team detected a nation-state attack on its corporate systems. The actor was **Midnight Blizzard**, Microsoft's name for the Russian state-sponsored group that the US and UK governments attribute to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR); other vendors call it APT29, UNC2452 or Cozy Bear, and it is the group behind the SolarWinds campaign retold in the federation course.

The name follows Microsoft's weather-based taxonomy for threat actors: the family name marks the origin (**Blizzard** means Russia; **Typhoon** means China), the adjective tells groups apart, **Tempest** marks financially motivated groups, and **Storm** plus a number is a temporary name for a group still being tracked.

This case uses everything from lessons 1 to 4: a tenant nobody watched, an app with more power than anyone remembered, and an application permission that opens every mailbox.

What Microsoft published (its MSRC post of 19 January and its Threat Intelligence guidance of 25 January 2024):

1. **Password spray**, beginning in late November 2023, against a *legacy, non-production test tenant*. The actor tried a few likely passwords against a limited number of accounts, with few attempts, from a **residential proxy** network (traffic routed through many home IP addresses also used by real people). One account fell: it had **no MFA**.
2. From there the actor found a **legacy test OAuth application that had elevated access to the Microsoft corporate environment**.
3. It **created additional malicious OAuth applications**, and **created a new user account** to grant consent to them in the corporate environment.
4. It used the legacy test app to grant its apps the Office 365 Exchange Online **`full_access_as_app`** role, which allows access to mailboxes through **EWS** (Exchange Web Services, Exchange's older web API).

**The result.** With those apps it read a very small percentage of Microsoft corporate mailboxes, including senior leadership, cybersecurity and legal staff, and exfiltrated some emails and attachments. Microsoft said it was initially looking for information about Midnight Blizzard itself.

blocks.title: From a forgotten test account to leadership mailboxes

scenes.caption: Low-and-slow password spray through residential proxies: few attempts per account, so no lockouts and no single bad IP to block.
The compromised test account leads to a legacy test OAuth app that, Microsoft said, had elevated access to the corporate environment.
The actor creates its own OAuth apps and a new user account in the corporate environment, which consents to those apps.
The legacy app grants the actor's apps full_access_as_app on Exchange Online: an application permission, so no user and no MFA are involved.
The apps authenticate as themselves and read targeted mailboxes over EWS, still through residential proxies.
Microsoft detected the attack on 12 January 2024, weeks after the spray began, and traced it by reviewing EWS activity in its audit logs.

blocks.md:
**Why each step worked.**

- *Non-production is still production for identity.* The test tenant was outside the controls of the corporate tenant. Microsoft wrote that if the same team deployed that tenant today, mandatory policy would ensure MFA and its active protections were enabled.
- *Apps outlive the people who made them.* A test app with corporate privileges gave the actor a non-human identity that could grant permissions.
- *Application permissions have no user to protect.* `full_access_as_app` covers mailboxes without anyone signing in, and Conditional Access scoped to users never runs for an app (lesson 10).
- *Residential proxies defeat IP blocklists.* Microsoft noted their high changeover rate makes IOC-based detection (indicators of compromise, such as known-bad IP addresses) infeasible, so detection had to be behavioural.

**Aftermath.** In March 2024 Microsoft reported that the actor was using information from the stolen email to gain, or try to gain, further access, which included access to some source code repositories and internal systems, and that its password sprays had increased by as much as 10-fold in February compared with January. Microsoft found no evidence that customer-facing systems were compromised, and stated the attack was not the result of a vulnerability in its products.

             "Application.ReadWrite.All", "Directory.ReadWrite.All"}

  {"t": "11-29 02:20", "activity": "Add application", "actor": "user:svc-sync7", "target": "app:mail-sync"},
  {"t": "11-29 02:31", "activity": "Consent to application", "actor": "user:svc-sync7", "target": "app:mail-sync"},
  {"t": "11-29 02:40", "activity": "Add app role assignment to service principal",
   "actor": "app:legacy-test-app", "target": "app:mail-sync", "role": "full_access_as_app"},
  {"t": "12-02 09:05", "activity": "Add app role assignment to service principal",
   "actor": "user:it-admin", "target": "app:hr-portal", "role": "User.Read.All"},
